Training Calibrated Conditional Generative Models with a Sample-Only Coverage Loss

Benjamin Remy Affiliation: NSF-Simons AI Institute for the Sky (SkAI) Affiliation: Department of Astronomy and Astrophysics, University of Chicago Affiliation: Kavli Institute for Cosmological Physics, University of Chicago    Raphael Rossellini Affiliation: Department of Statistics, University of Chicago    Chihway Chang Affiliation: NSF-Simons AI Institute for the Sky (SkAI) Affiliation: Department of Astronomy and Astrophysics, University of Chicago Affiliation: Kavli Institute for Cosmological Physics, University of Chicago    Rebecca Willett Affiliation: NSF-Simons AI Institute for the Sky (SkAI) Affiliation: Department of Statistics, University of Chicago Affiliation: NSF-Simons National Institute for Theory and Mathematics in Biology (NITMB) Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Chicago
Abstract

Conditional generative models have become the tool of choice for sampling posteriors in scientific inverse problems, where we seek to sample images or signals conditioned on a set of indirect and noisy measurements. Yet they are often overconfident, which is a critical failure in scientific applications where accurate uncertainty quantification is essential. Existing regularizers fall short in complementary ways: differentiable coverage objectives require the model’s density and do not identify the posterior, while strictly proper scoring rules such as the energy score need only samples but do not directly enforce coverage. We close this gap by introducing a differentiable loss function based on the expected coverage probability, estimated from samples alone. It applies to any conditional generative model, with no need for tractable densities or architectural changes. We prove that it is a strict divergence, vanishing if and only if the model equals the true posterior. On simulation-based inference benchmarks, it matches a density-based coverage loss without evaluating the density. On high-dimensional imaging inverse problems, it yields better-calibrated posteriors than scoring-rule regularizers, with little change in the reconstruction quality of point estimates.

1 Introduction

Inverse problems are ubiquitous across scientific domains, including medical imaging (Liu et al., 2009), astrophysics (Adam et al., 2022; Remy et al., 2023), engineering (Melia et al., 2025), and economics (Horowitz, 2014). Measurements of the signal of interest are typically acquired indirectly, only partially, and corrupted by noise, making the recovery of the underlying parameters ill-posed. Many different parameters can explain the same observations, so we seek to sample from the full range of admissible signals; such samples enable uncertainty quantification.

Bayesian inference provides a principled framework for this, modeling the set of all plausible solutions through the posterior distribution of the parameters given the observations. Deep generative models have made it possible to learn this posterior from pairs of parameters and corresponding measurements. Normalizing Flows (Rezende and Mohamed, 2015; Papamakarios et al., 2021, NF,), generative adversarial networks (Goodfellow et al., 2014, GANs,), and more recently diffusion (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021b) and flow (Lipman et al., 2022; Albergo et al., 2025) models have all been successful at conditional sampling. However, each of these models has known failure modes that produce unreliable posteriors. GANs are prone to mode collapse (Metz et al., 2016), and NFs have been shown to be frequently overconfident for posteriors (Hermans et al., 2022). Diffusion models, while achieving remarkable sample quality, have also been found to under-represent the uncertainty of the true posterior (Yao et al., 2026).

We seek models with valid conditional coverage: for every measurement yy and every level α\alpha, whenever the model assigns probability α\alpha to a region of signals, the true signal should fall in that region with probability α\alpha under the posterior p⁡(θ∣y)p(\theta\mid y), that is, α⋅100%\alpha\cdot 100\% of the time over hypothetical draws of the true signal conditioned on that measurement. Requiring conditional coverage for all regions is equivalent to the learned posterior estimate qϕ(⋅∣y)q_{\phi}(\cdot\mid y) equaling the true posterior p(⋅∣y)p(\cdot\mid y), but it cannot be checked directly, since a dataset typically contains a single ground-truth signal per measurement.

Two families of training objectives address this problem, each with a complementary weakness. Coverage objectives (Delaunoy et al., 2022; Falkiewicz et al., 2023) add to the training loss a differentiable measure of the estimator’s coverage, typically computed on its highest probability density (HPD) regions, or a constraint favoring conservative estimators. They target coverage directly, but they have two limitations. Computing HPD regions requires evaluating the estimator density, which restricts these methods to architectures with tractable likelihoods, such as NFs, and excludes diffusion models and GANs. Moreover, they enforce marginal coverage, which does not identify the posterior: many distributions, including the prior, have valid marginal coverage. Strictly proper scoring rules, such as the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) or the energy score, require only samples and are uniquely minimized at the posterior, but they do not target coverage, and in practice they can yield poorly calibrated models due to finite-sample effects, model misspecification and the geometry of the loss landscape (Section 2).

The basic idea is to assess a conditional generative model by asking how much of its probability mass lies closer to a reference point than the true signal does. For a given measurement yy, choose a reference point ψ⁡(y)\psi(y) and consider balls centered at this point. The model assigns a probability mass to each ball, and we can check how often the true signal falls inside it. If the model is correct, the two agree at every probability level, and we measure departures from this agreement with a Cramér–von Mises (CvM) discrepancy. This construction builds on TARP (Tests of Accuracy with Random Points, Lemos et al., 2023), and we call the resulting loss TARP-CvM. The converse depends on how reference points are chosen. A reference rule assigns a reference point to every measurement, and a single rule is not enough, even one that depends on the measurement. Its coverage is averaged over measurements, so over-coverage at some measurements can balance under-coverage at others. We therefore compute the discrepancy separately for many rules and average the discrepancies, rather than pooling their coverage. Our main theoretical result shows that if the rules can place reference points anywhere and can differ across regions of measurement space, this average vanishes only when the model equals the true posterior. Our contributions are:

  • •

    Theory: a sufficient condition on the distribution of measurement-dependent reference rules under which our TARP-CvM loss vanishes if and only if the model equals the true posterior.

  • •

    Algorithm: a sample-only, differentiable estimator of TARP-CvM that applies to any conditional generative model, together with a practical construction of reference rules that satisfies this condition.

  • •

    Experiments: on simulation-based inference, TARP-CvM matches a density-based coverage loss without evaluating the density; on high-dimensional imaging inverse problems, it is the only regularizer we tested that brings the posterior into the Mira null band on all three problems, with little change in the quality of point estimates.

Problem formulation.

We seek to recover parameters θ∈Θ⊆ℝdθ\theta\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{\theta}} from indirect measurements y∈𝒴⊆ℝdyy\in{\cal Y}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}. Knowledge of the data likelihood p⁡(y∣θ)p(y\mid\theta) may be used to generate training samples but is not otherwise required. There may exist a forward model 𝒜\mathcal{A} such that y=𝒜⁡(θ)+εy=\mathcal{A}(\theta)+\varepsilon, where ε\varepsilon is a noise vector, and together 𝒜{\cal A} and the distribution of ε\varepsilon control the data likelihood p⁡(y∣θ)p(y\mid\theta). This setting encompasses a wide range of problems: in inverse problems, θ\theta may be a high-dimensional image of a patient’s anatomy, yy the raw measurements collected by an MRI scanner, and 𝒜\mathcal{A} a model of the scanner’s measurement process; in simulation-based inference, θ\theta may be the parameters of a physics simulation, with 𝒜\mathcal{A} the simulator itself, in which case we seek to infer θ\theta from observations yy. We seek to sample from the posterior distribution p⁡(θ∣y)p(\theta\mid y), but cannot evaluate the prior density p⁡(θ)p(\theta). We have only samples, a training set {(θ1,y1),…,(θn,yn)}\{(\theta_{1},y_{1}),\ldots,(\theta_{n},y_{n})\} of nn pairs drawn from the joint distribution p⁡(θ,y)p(\theta,y), so that the θi\theta_{i} are samples from the prior. Our strategy is to train a conditional generative model, denoted qϕ(⋅|y)q_{\phi}(\cdot|y), which takes as input a measurement vector yy and a random seed and generates a sample θ\theta, where ϕ∈ℝp\phi\in\mathbb{R}^{p} is the vector of generative model parameters (e.g., neural network weights) to be learned.

2 Related work

Generative models for inverse problems

Model-agnostic methods train a conditional generative model on paired samples (θi,yi)(\theta_{i},y_{i}), without using the forward model 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Model-adaptive methods instead combine a generative prior over θ\theta, pre-trained without measurements, with knowledge of 𝒜\mathcal{A} at sampling time, as in Diffusion Posterior Sampling (Chung et al., 2022). We focus on the model-agnostic setting, but the core ideas translate naturally to model-adaptive samplers.

Coverage tests

Two standard approaches for empirically testing coverage of qϕq_{\phi} are Highest Posterior Density (Hermans et al., 2022, HPD,) testing and Tests of Accuracy with Random Points (Lemos et al., 2023, TARP,). HPD testing constructs, for each test point yy, the smallest region C⊂ℝdθC\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{\theta}} under qϕ(⋅∣y)q_{\phi}(\cdot\mid y) that contains α\alpha probability mass, and then checks whether the true θ\theta falls inside that region at the expected rate. However, HPD requires evaluating the density of qϕq_{\phi}, which is often unavailable for generative models, and valid HPD coverage is not a sufficient condition for accuracy: a model can pass the HPD test while still differing from the posterior. Fig. 1 illustrates the limitations of using HPD to train a conditional generative model vis-à-vis our proposed measure, TARP-CvM; details on this experiment are in Section 5.1.

TARP instead constructs regions as balls centered at randomly chosen reference points, measuring coverage by the fraction of samples from qϕ(⋅∣y)q_{\phi}(\cdot\mid y) that fall closer to the reference point than the true θ\theta does. Lemos et al. (2023) show that correct TARP coverage for every assignment of reference points to measurements is necessary and sufficient for the estimator to equal the posterior, so TARP can detect errors that HPD-based tests miss, while requiring only samples from qϕq_{\phi} rather than density evaluations. The key distinction is that HPD regions are implicitly centered by the geometry of the estimated density, whereas TARP regions can be centered at arbitrary reference points. This flexibility lets TARP probe aspects of the posterior that HPD coverage cannot capture. Which assignments are needed in practice is left open; we make this precise in Section 3. The output of TARP is a coverage curve that plots the empirical coverage rate against the nominal credibility level α\alpha, with a perfectly calibrated model lying on the diagonal. Although correct TARP coverage for every possible assignment of reference points characterizes the posterior, this does not immediately provide a practical training objective. In particular, averaging coverage over randomly chosen reference points can conceal errors, because overcoverage and undercoverage may cancel. Our contribution is to identify a tractable family of reference rules whose individual coverage discrepancies can be averaged without losing the ability to identify the posterior.

Because TARP produces a coverage curve rather than a scalar, it does not directly support quantitative comparisons between models. Mira (Sharief et al., 2026) provides such a scalar. Over many randomly drawn regions and joint samples (θ,y)∼p⁡(θ,y)(\theta,y)\sim p(\theta,y), it estimates the probability that the true θ\theta falls in a region given the fraction of samples from qϕ(⋅∣y)q_{\phi}(\cdot\mid y) that fall in it. Under calibration, the Mira score equals 2/32/3, and values below this level indicate overconfidence. Since our loss is built on TARP, evaluating it with TARP coverage alone would be partly circular. We therefore use Mira as an independent metric: it relies on its own random regions, is not optimized by any of the methods we compare, and provides a calibrated reference value with a null band that accounts for sampling noise.

Energy Score and CRPS

Using MSE as a loss function assesses a model’s ability to correctly estimate the conditional mean, but it does not reward modeling the spread of possibilities correctly and can prefer overconfident generators. The Energy Score (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007, ES, )

ES(qϕ(⋅|y),θ)=2𝔼θ^∼qϕ(⋅|y)∥θ^−θ∥2−𝔼θ^,θ^′∼qϕ(⋅|y)∥θ^−θ^′∥2,\mathrm{ES}(q_{\phi}(\cdot|y),\theta)=2\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\theta}\sim q_{\phi}(\cdot|y)}\|\hat{\theta}-\theta\|_{2}-\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\theta},\hat{\theta}^{\prime}\sim q_{\phi}(\cdot|y)}\|\hat{\theta}-\hat{\theta}^{\prime}\|_{2},

addresses this by penalizing samples far from the true θ\theta while rewarding spread. It is strictly proper on distributions with finite first moment, with expectation under p(⋅∣y)p(\cdot\mid y) uniquely minimized at qϕ(⋅∣y)=p(⋅∣y)q_{\phi}(\cdot\mid y)=p(\cdot\mid y), and it can be estimated from samples alone. Its univariate case is the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS). In high dimension, the CRPS is often summed over coordinates (pCRPS), which parallelizes across pixels, but only identifies the marginals of the posterior. Strict propriety says that the population objective has the true posterior as its unique global minimizer. It does not guarantee that training finds this minimizer. The loss is estimated on finite batches and minimized by gradient descent, which can stop at local minima, and if the model class does not contain the posterior, the guarantee says nothing about which approximation is found. Training with a strictly proper scoring rule therefore need not produce a calibrated model.

Two objectives can share the same global minimizer but have very different landscapes. In a Gaussian toy model, the energy score is much flatter than TARP-CvM in the direction of the posterior spread when the mean is biased, so that noisy gradients are less likely to correct the spread, whereas TARP-CvM penalizes miscoverage directly (Appendix D.3). Our experiments reflect this difference; on most of our imaging inverse problems, ES and pCRPS improve coverage but remain overconfident, whereas TARP-CvM reaches calibration (Section 5.2).

Calibration objectives

Several works have proposed training objectives that encourage calibration directly, including the HPD objective of Falkiewicz et al. (2023), the rank-based statistics of Yao et al. (2024), and the balanced NRE approach of Delaunoy et al. (2022), which favors conservative rather than exactly calibrated estimators. These methods target marginal calibration, which does not ensure calibration conditionally on the measurement (Kuleshov et al., 2018). Conformal prediction (Angelopoulos and Bates, 2023) instead acts after training: using a held-out calibration set, it turns the predictions of any trained model into sets that contain the true value with a chosen probability, without assumptions on the data distribution and for any calibration set size. This guarantee is also marginal, since conditional coverage is unattainable in this distribution-free setting, and the procedure does not provide a loss or score that can be used to train the model. Conditioning the calibration statistic on yy gives a stronger notion of calibration, explored both as a diagnostic (Zhao et al., 2021) and for post-hoc recalibration (Dey et al., 2025). Our loss enforces it during training, at the population level.

3 The TARP-CvM loss: A strict divergence

This section builds the TARP-CvM loss in three stages. We first describe how the TARP coverage test of Lemos et al. (2023) assesses a conditional generative model: it centers a ball at a reference point chosen from the measurement, measures how much of the estimator’s mass lies closer to the reference point than the true parameter does, and checks whether these masses are uniformly distributed (Section 3.1). We then relate this test to credible regions and to the expected coverage probability, which places TARP alongside HPD-based tests (Section 3.2). Finally, we turn the test into a population objective and give conditions under which it vanishes only at the true posterior (Section 3.3).

3.1 The TARP construction

TARP replaces the HPD level sets of the density (Section 2) by balls, whose mass can be estimated from samples alone. Given a pair (θ,y)(\theta,y) drawn from the joint distribution p⁡(θ,y)p(\theta,y), for instance a training pair (θi,yi)(\theta_{i},y_{i}), the construction proceeds in four steps.

Step 1: choose a reference point. For the measurement yy, choose a reference point ψ⁡(y)∈Θ\psi(y)\in\Theta. Since this choice must be made for every measurement, we formalize it as a rule.

Definition 1 (Reference rule).

A reference rule is a measurable map ψ:𝒴→Θ\psi:\mathcal{Y}\to\Theta that assigns to each measurement yy a single reference point ψ⁡(y)\psi(y). A rule is deterministic and specifies the reference points of all measurements jointly. Randomness over reference points enters only through a distribution ρ\rho over rules (Definition 4).

Step 2: construct a ball. Center a ball at ψ⁡(y)\psi(y), with radius chosen so that the ball just contains the true θ\theta, that is, the ball B⁡(ψ⁡(y),d⁡(θ,ψ⁡(y)))B\big(\psi(y),d(\theta,\psi(y))\big), where dd is a distance on Θ\Theta and B⁡(c,r)={θ~:d⁡(θ~,c)≤r}B(c,r)=\{\tilde{\theta}:d(\tilde{\theta},c)\leq r\} is the closed ball.

Step 3: evaluate its mass under the estimator. Define the credibility value as the probability mass of this ball, where the probability is with respect to the distribution qϕ(⋅∣y)q_{\phi}(\cdot\mid y):

sψ(θ,y)=ℙqϕ​(θ~∣y)[d(θ~,ψ(y))≤d(θ,ψ(y))].s_{\psi}(\theta,y)=\mathbb{P}_{q_{\phi}(\tilde{\theta}\mid y)}\!\left[d(\tilde{\theta},\psi(y))\leq d(\theta,\psi(y))\right].

In practice, it is the fraction of draws θ~∼qϕ(⋅∣y)\tilde{\theta}\sim q_{\phi}(\cdot\mid y) that fall inside the ball (see Figure 2b).

Step 4: evaluate coverage. Repeating Steps 1–3 over pairs (θ,y)∼p⁡(θ,y)(\theta,y)\sim p(\theta,y), with the same rule ψ\psi, gives a distribution of credibility values. The conditional coverage of rule ψ\psi at measurement yy and the marginal coverage, its average over measurements, are

Fψ​(α∣y)\displaystyle F_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y) =ℙp⁡(θ∣y)[sψ(θ,y)≤α]\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}_{p(\theta\mid y)}\big[s_{\psi}(\theta,y)\leq\alpha\big] (conditional coverage),\displaystyle\text{(conditional coverage)}, (1)
Fψ​(α)\displaystyle F_{\psi}(\alpha) =𝔼p⁡(y)​[Fψ​(α∣y)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p(y)}\big[F_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y)\big] (marginal coverage).\displaystyle\text{(marginal coverage)}. (2)

Since Fψ​(α∣y)F_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y) depends on ψ\psi only through the reference point ψ⁡(y)\psi(y), we also write Fc​(α∣y)F_{c}(\alpha\mid y) for the coverage at yy of balls centered at a point c∈Θc\in\Theta, so that Fψ​(α∣y)=Fψ⁡(y)​(α∣y)F_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y)=F_{\psi(y)}(\alpha\mid y). If the estimated posterior is correct, the credibility values of the true parameters are uniformly distributed on [0,1][0,1] at every measurement, Fψ​(α∣y)=αF_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y)=\alpha (Lemma 1 below). The original TARP test pools the credibility values over randomly drawn reference points. We instead compare them to the uniform distribution separately for each rule and average the resulting discrepancies (Section 3.3).

3.2 Credible regions and expected coverage

To relate TARP to HPD-based tests, we view the balls of Section 3.1 as credible regions of the estimator and their marginal coverage Fψ​(α)F_{\psi}(\alpha) as an expected coverage probability.

Definition 2 (Adapted from Lemos et al. (2023)).

Assumption 1.

Θ⊆ℝdθ\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_{\theta}} is open, and for every yy, p(⋅∣y)p(\cdot\mid y) and qϕ(⋅∣y)q_{\phi}(\cdot\mid y) have continuous densities that are strictly positive on Θ\Theta.

Lemma 1.

Under Assumption 1, if qϕ(⋅∣y)=p(⋅∣y)q_{\phi}(\cdot\mid y)=p(\cdot\mid y) for every yy, then Fψ​(α∣y)=αF_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y)=\alpha for every rule ψ\psi, for every level α\alpha and every yy, and hence Fψ​(α)=αF_{\psi}(\alpha)=\alpha.

In other words, a correct estimator is always calibrated, no matter how the regions are chosen (Proof in Appendix A). However the converse, calibration for a map implies qϕ=pq_{\phi}=p, depends on the choice of the map, and is the central question of Section 3.3.

3.3 The population objective

Definition 4.

For a distribution ρ\rho over reference rules, we introduce the loss function

𝒟ρ​(p,qϕ)=𝔼ψ∼ρ​∫01(Fψ​(α)−α)2​𝑑α.\mathcal{D}_{\rho}(p,q_{\phi})=\mathbb{E}_{\psi\sim\rho}\int_{0}^{1}\left(F_{\psi}(\alpha)-\alpha\right)^{2}d\alpha. (4)

𝒟ρ=0\mathcal{D}_{\rho}=0 iff the estimator is calibrated for every rule ψ\psi in the support of ρ\rho. For a single rule, the integrand compares each credibility level α\alpha with the frequency Fψ​(α)F_{\psi}(\alpha) at which the true parameter falls in the corresponding region. The inner integral is thus a continuous analogue of the expected calibration error used in classification (Naeini et al., 2015), and closely resembles the calibration error of Kuleshov et al. (2018) for regression. The outer expectation over rules is what distinguishes it from these per-model calibration scores, and the choice of ρ\rho determines the properties of 𝒟ρ\mathcal{D}_{\rho}. We motivate the requirements on ρ\rho below and formalize them in Definition 6.

For a fixed rule ψ\psi, the integral is the Cramér–von Mises distance (Cramér, 1928) DCvM(X1,X2)=∫01(ℙ[X1≤α]−ℙ[X2≤α])2dαD_{\rm CvM}(X_{1},X_{2})=\int_{0}^{1}\big(\mathbb{P}[X_{1}\leq\alpha]-\mathbb{P}[X_{2}\leq\alpha]\big)^{2}d\alpha, where X1=sψ​(θ,y)X_{1}=s_{\psi}(\theta,y), the credibility of the true parameters, whose CDF is FψF_{\psi}, and X2∼𝒰⁡[0,1]X_{2}\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1] is the uniform distribution. 𝒟ρ\mathcal{D}_{\rho} is non-negative and, under Assumption 1 and for any admissible ρ\rho (Definition 6), vanishes if and only if qϕ=pq_{\phi}=p (Theorem 1); in this sense it is a divergence between conditional distributions. It is not a metric, since it is not symmetric in (p,qϕ)(p,q_{\phi}) and does not satisfy the triangle inequality, and it is not a scoring rule, since it is quadratic in the distribution of (θ,y)(\theta,y) rather than an average of per-example scores.

Constant reference points cannot identify the posterior.

A rule that ignores the measurement lets the prior pass the coverage test. Let us consider a constant rule ψ⁡(y)=c\psi(y)=c. If our estimator returns the prior, qϕ​(θ∣y)=p⁡(θ)q_{\phi}(\theta\mid y)=p(\theta), the TARP region Rα,ψTARP​(y)=Rα,cTARPR^{\text{TARP}}_{\alpha,\psi}(y)=R^{\text{TARP}}_{\alpha,c} no longer depends on yy, since both its center and the distribution defining its radius are fixed. Then ECP⁡(qϕ,α,Rα,ψTARP)=𝔼p⁡(θ,y)​[𝟏θ∈Rα,cTARP]=∫p⁡(y)​∫Rα,cTARPp⁡(θ∣y)​𝑑θ​𝑑y=∫Rα,cTARP(∫p⁡(θ∣y)​p​(y)​𝑑y)​𝑑θ=∫Rα,cTARPp⁡(θ)​𝑑θ\mathrm{ECP}(q_{\phi},\alpha,R^{\text{TARP}}_{\alpha,\psi})=\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta,y)}\big[\mathbf{1}_{\theta\in R^{\text{TARP}}_{\alpha,c}}\big]=\int p(y)\int_{R^{\text{TARP}}_{\alpha,c}}p(\theta\mid y)\,d\theta\,dy=\int_{R^{\text{TARP}}_{\alpha,c}}\left(\int p(\theta\mid y)p(y)\,dy\right)d\theta=\int_{R^{\text{TARP}}_{\alpha,c}}p(\theta)\,d\theta.. Since qϕ​(θ∣y)=p⁡(θ)q_{\phi}(\theta\mid y)=p(\theta) and by definition of a credible region, we get ECP⁡(qϕ,α,Rα,ψTARP)=α\mathrm{ECP}(q_{\phi},\alpha,R^{\text{TARP}}_{\alpha,\psi})=\alpha, which evaluates the estimator as calibrated.

A single measurement-dependent rule is still insufficient.

Reference points must depend on the measurement, but this alone does not guarantee that the loss identifies the posterior. A single rule gives each measurement its own reference point, but its coverage Fψ​(α)=∫Fψ​(α∣y)​p​(y)​𝑑yF_{\psi}(\alpha)=\int F_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y)\,p(y)\,dy is an average over measurements, and errors at different measurements can cancel. Suppose there are two measurements y0y_{0} and y1y_{1}, each with probability 12\frac{1}{2}, and an estimator that is too wide at y0y_{0} and too narrow at y1y_{1}, with Fψ​(α∣yι)=α+(−1)ι​δ​α​(1−α)F_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y_{\iota})=\alpha+(-1)^{\iota}\delta\,\alpha(1-\alpha) for ι∈{0,1}\iota\in\{0,1\} and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). The coverage curves at y0y_{0} and y1y_{1} deviate from the diagonal in opposite directions and average to it, so Fψ​(α)=αF_{\psi}(\alpha)=\alpha at every level: the estimator is calibrated under ψ\psi yet wrong at both measurements. Choosing a better single rule does not help, since the counterexample holds for any ψ\psi.

Comparing rules requires local differences.

For a wrong estimator, the conditional coverage Fψ​(α∣y)F_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y) (Equation 1) depends on where the ball is centered, so errors can be revealed by comparing different reference points at the same measurement. The loss, however, only sees marginal coverages Fψ​(α)F_{\psi}(\alpha), so this comparison must be made across several rules. It isolates a subset of measurements only if the collection contains pairs of rules that agree on most measurements and differ on that subset: the difference between their marginal coverages then depends only on the subset. If every pair of rules differs at all measurements, errors can still cancel within each marginal average.

For instance, a simpler reference would add noise to a point estimate b⁡(y)b(y) at scale ς\varsigma (see Section 4.2 for definitions), ψ⁡(yi)=b⁡(yi)+ς​ξi\psi(y_{i})=b(y_{i})+\varsigma\xi_{i}, with ξi\xi_{i} drawn either independently for each example or once for the whole batch. Neither is sufficient. With independent draws, the batch yields a single coverage curve, F¯​(α)=∫𝔼ξ​[Fb⁡(y)+ς​ξ​(α∣y)]​p​(y)​𝑑y\bar{F}(\alpha)=\int\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[F_{b(y)+\varsigma\xi}(\alpha\mid y)\big]\,p(y)\,dy, and a single statistic ∫01(F¯​(α)−α)2​𝑑α\int_{0}^{1}\big(\bar{F}(\alpha)-\alpha\big)^{2}\,d\alpha. The expectation over reference points then sits inside the square of Equation 4, and the examples where Fb⁡(yi)+ς​ξi​(α∣yi)>αF_{b(y_{i})+\varsigma\xi_{i}}(\alpha\mid y_{i})>\alpha can balance those where Fb⁡(yi)+ς​ξi​(α∣yi)<αF_{b(y_{i})+\varsigma\xi_{i}}(\alpha\mid y_{i})<\alpha, so that F¯​(α)=α\bar{F}(\alpha)=\alpha even if Fb⁡(yi)+ς​ξi​(α∣yi)≠αF_{b(y_{i})+\varsigma\xi_{i}}(\alpha\mid y_{i})\neq\alpha for every example. If instead a single displacement ξr\xi_{r} is shared by the batch, each draw is a rule ψr​(y)=b⁡(y)+ς​ξr\psi_{r}(y)=b(y)+\varsigma\xi_{r} giving a statistic IψrI_{\psi_{r}}, and the rules satisfy (R1) below. But each IψrI_{\psi_{r}} constrains Fψr​(α∣y)F_{\psi_{r}}(\alpha\mid y) only through an average over all measurements, so nothing prevents over-coverage at some measurements from balancing under-coverage at others for every ξr\xi_{r} at once, and Theorem 1 does not apply to these rules.

Patching rules resolves the problem.

Given two reference rules, a patched rule uses the first rule for measurements on one side of a hyperplane and the second rule for measurements on the other side. Thus, we can change the reference points for one subset of measurements while leaving the rest unchanged. In the example above, with δ=0.8\delta=0.8 and α=12\alpha=\frac{1}{2}, the coverages are 0.70.7 and 0.30.3 under ψ\psi; take a second calibrated rule ψ′\psi^{\prime}, centered elsewhere, with coverages 0.60.6 and 0.40.4. Switching rules across measurements, ψ\psi at y0y_{0} and ψ′\psi^{\prime} at y1y_{1}, gives 12​(0.7+0.4)=0.55\frac{1}{2}(0.7+0.4)=0.55, and the miscalibration appears.

Definition 5.

For rules ψ,ψ′\psi,\psi^{\prime} and a measurable set H⊆𝒴H\subseteq\mathcal{Y}, the patched rule uses ψ\psi on HH and ψ′\psi^{\prime} elsewhere, (ψ⊕Hψ′)(y)=ψ(y) 1y∈H+ψ′(y) 1y∉H(\psi\oplus_{H}\psi^{\prime})(y)=\psi(y)\,\mathbf{1}_{y\in H}+\psi^{\prime}(y)\,\mathbf{1}_{y\notin H}.

Patching along all half-spaces is enough (Lemma 5), which is condition (R2) below. The reference rules must have two properties. First, at every measurement, the available reference points must be sufficiently rich to probe the entire parameter space. Second, the collection of rules must allow reference points to be changed on arbitrary half-spaces of measurement space while remaining unchanged elsewhere. These two properties ensure that coverage errors cannot be hidden by averaging, and that the resulting coverage tests distinguish different conditional distributions.

Definition 6.

A distribution ρ\rho over rules is admissible if there exists a countable family of rules Ψ⊆supp⁡ρ\Psi\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\rho (Appendix A.1) such that

  • (R1)

    For every yy, the centers {ψ⁡(y):ψ∈Ψ}\{\psi(y):\psi\in\Psi\} are dense in Θ\Theta.

  • (R2)

    For all ψ,ψ′∈Ψ\psi,\psi^{\prime}\in\Psi and every half-space H={y:⟨u,y⟩≤t}H=\{y:\langle u,y\rangle\leq t\}, with uu a unit vector of ℝdy\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}} and t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, the patched rule ψ⊕Hψ′\psi\oplus_{H}\psi^{\prime} is in supp⁡ρ\operatorname{supp}\rho.

With (R1), the loss can place reference points anywhere near the posterior mass at each measurement. With (R2), they may be used on the two sides of a hyperplane in measurement space, which is enough to tell measurements apart.

The switch rule of Equation 8 avoids both problems of the noisy point estimate above. Because each side of the hyperplane shares one displacement, each draw is a rule with its own statistic. Using one displacement on HH and another on its complement changes the reference points of the measurements in HH only, so errors inside HH can no longer be balanced by errors outside it. Calibration of every such rule, for every HH, forces the coverage at almost every measurement to be the same for every displacement (condition (R2) and Lemma 5).

Definition 7.

The TARP-CvM loss is Equation 4 for an admissible ρ\rho.

Theorem 1 (TARP–CvM is a strict divergence).

Under Assumption 1 and for any admissible ρ\rho, 𝒟ρ​(p,qϕ)=0\mathcal{D}_{\rho}(p,q_{\phi})=0 if and only if qϕ(⋅∣y)=p(⋅∣y)q_{\phi}(\cdot\mid y)=p(\cdot\mid y) for almost all yy.

Proof in Appendix A. The direction qϕ=p⇒𝒟ρ=0q_{\phi}=p\Rightarrow\mathcal{D}_{\rho}=0 follows from Lemma 1. The converse proceeds in three steps. First, zero loss implies calibration for every rule in the support of ρ\rho. Second, patching (R2) implies that the conditional coverage at almost every measurement does not depend on the reference point. Third, since reference points are dense (R1), this invariance holds only if the estimated and true posteriors agree.

Lemos et al. (2023, Theorem 3) show that a posterior estimator is exact if its expected coverage is correct for every function assigning reference points to measurements. Their argument relies on a functional derivative with respect to this function. They do not specify how reference points should be selected from the measurement, and in their experiments reference points are drawn independently of it, a setting in which the prior also passes the test. Moreover, the original TARP pools coverage over randomly drawn reference points, and the pooled coverage can match the nominal level even when a distribution is miscalibrated with respect to an individual rule, because their errors can cancel in the average. Theorem 1 shows how our TARP-CvM addresses both issues. It gives an explicit sufficient condition on how reference points depend on the measurement (Definition 6). Our loss averages the miscalibration of a distribution with respect to each rule rather than pooling, so that zero loss implies calibration for every rule in the support.

4 Making the objective trainable

At each training iteration, we draw a batch of paired observations and ground-truth signals (θi,yi)(\theta_{i},y_{i}), generate samples for each observation θ~i,m\tilde{\theta}_{i,m}, and construct several reference rules. For each rule, we compute the credibility of every ground-truth signal θi\theta_{i} relative to the corresponding generated samples. We then calculate a Cramér–von Mises discrepancy between the empirical distribution of these credibility values and the uniform distribution. The average discrepancy over reference rules is added to the base generative-model training loss.

4.1 The closed form estimator

The objective term in Equation 4 is the squared area Iψ=∫01(Fψ​(α)−α)2​𝑑αI_{\psi}=\int_{0}^{1}\left(F_{\psi}(\alpha)-\alpha\right)^{2}d\alpha between the cumulative distribution function of the credibility values and the diagonal. FψF_{\psi} is empirically estimated with NN credibility values si=sψ​(θi,yi)s_{i}=s_{\psi}(\theta_{i},y_{i}) from pairs (θi,yi)(\theta_{i},y_{i}) of the batch, F^ψ​(α)≈1N​∑i𝟏si≤α\hat{F}_{\psi}(\alpha)\approx\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}_{s_{i}\leq\alpha}, computed with the same rule ψ\psi. IψI_{\psi} is a Cramér-von Mises statistic, and its derivative admits a closed-form expression (Yao et al., 2024). The statistic measures the squared discrepancy between the empirical distribution of the credibility values and the uniform distribution. The usual integral representation involves indicator functions and is not convenient for gradient-based optimization. By integrating analytically over the credibility levels, we obtain the following expression in terms of the sorted credibility values. See Appendix C for details on deriving this empirical estimator:

CvM(s1:N)=1N∑isi2−1N2∑k=1N(2k−1)s(k)+13,\mathrm{CvM}(s_{1:N})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}s_{i}^{2}-\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{k=1}^{N}(2k-1)\,s_{(k)}+\frac{1}{3}, (5)

where s(1)≤⋯≤s(N)s_{(1)}\leq\dots\leq s_{(N)} are the sorted credibility values. Writing rank⁡(i)\operatorname{rank}(i) for the position of sis_{i} in this ordering, so that si=s(rank⁡(i))s_{i}=s_{(\operatorname{rank}(i))}, the gradient is

∂CvM∂si=2​siN−2​rank​(i)−1N2.\frac{\partial\mathrm{CvM}}{\partial s_{i}}=\frac{2s_{i}}{N}-\frac{2\,\mathrm{rank}(i)-1}{N^{2}}. (6)

The closed form expression is what makes the statistic differentiable, by turning evaluation on a grid of levels α\alpha, where most indicator counts would have zero gradient, into a polynomial of the sorted values. Integrating over α\alpha first removes the indicators, and the resulting expression depends on sis_{i} values and rank. It was used by Yao et al. (2024) to turn a rank-uniformity test into a differentiable objective for simulation-based inference. We differ in the choice of the statistic. Coordinate-wise ranks constrain only the one-dimensional marginals of the estimator, so the prior estimator also passes the test, whereas uniformity of the credibility value across admissible rules forces the estimator to equal the posterior as stated in Theorem 1.

Unbiased estimator

Equation 5 is the plug-in estimate of the inner integral of Equation 4. Written as an average over all pairs (i,j)(i,j) of credibility values, it includes the diagonal pairs i=ji=j, so its expectation exceeds it by 1N​∫01Fψ​(1−Fψ)​𝑑α\frac{1}{N}\int_{0}^{1}F_{\psi}(1-F_{\psi})\,d\alpha, a term that does not vanish at the posterior. Excluding the diagonal pairs gives an unbiased U-statistic (Hoeffding, 1948),

CvMU(s1:N)=1N∑isi2−2N⁡(N−1)∑k=1N(k−1)s(k)+13.\mathrm{CvM}_{U}(s_{1:N})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}s_{i}^{2}-\frac{2}{N(N-1)}\sum_{k=1}^{N}(k-1)\,s_{(k)}+\frac{1}{3}. (7)

Equation 7is therefore preferable when an unbiased estimate of the population discrepancy is desired (Proposition 2, see Appendix C for derivation). In our experiments, however, we use the simpler plug-in statistic in Equation 5. Its finite-sample bias is not removed, but the same estimator is used consistently throughout training.

4.2 Reference points

The objective Equation 4 is an average over reference rules. Each optimization step draws RR rules and applies each one to every pair in the batch. It then computes the CvM statistic of Equation 5 separately for each rule and averages the RR statistics. This keeps the expectation over rules outside the squared deviation, as in Equation 4. The rules are drawn from a mixture of three groups: switch rules, prior rules and posterior rules.

Switch rules.

Figure 2 illustrates the construction. A switch rule needs a point estimate b⁡(y)b(y) with nontrivial posterior likelihood. For a linear forward model y=A​θ+εy=A\theta+\varepsilon, we take the adjoint reconstruction b⁡(y)=A⊤​yb(y)=A^{\top}y, or the pseudo-inverse A+​yA^{+}y. Without an adjoint, bb can be a regressor of the posterior mean, trained beforehand on the same pairs (Section 5.3). A switch rule splits the measurements of the batch with a hyperplane and displaces the point estimate by one displacement on one side and by another on the other side, so that it is a single rule patched across a half-space (Definition 5). It is determined by two displacements ξ,ξ′\xi,\xi^{\prime}, a unit vector uu in measurement space that orients the hyperplane, and an example jj of the batch through which it passes, and assigns to every example yiy_{i} the reference point

ψ⁡(yi)=b⁡(yi)+ς⁡(ξ​ 1⟨u,yi⟩≤⟨u,yj⟩+ξ′​ 1⟨u,yi⟩>⟨u,yj⟩),\psi(y_{i})=b(y_{i})+\varsigma\left(\xi\,\mathbf{1}_{\langle u,y_{i}\rangle\leq\langle u,y_{j}\rangle}+\xi^{\prime}\,\mathbf{1}_{\langle u,y_{i}\rangle>\langle u,y_{j}\rangle}\right), (8)

where ς∈ℝ>0dθ\varsigma\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\theta}}_{>0} is a fixed reference scale, applied component-wise and treated as a constant. Drawing ξ,ξ′∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\xi,\xi^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), a random unit vector uu and a random example jj chooses a switch rule at random; once drawn, it is a fixed rule in the sense of Definition 1. In our experiments, we set ς\varsigma to the root-mean-square residual of bb on a held-out tenth of the training simulations,

ς=(𝔼⁡[(b⁡(y)−θ)2])1/2,\varsigma=\big(\mathbb{E}\big[(b(y)-\theta)^{2}\big]\big)^{1/2}, (9)

with the square and root taken element-wise, so that the reference displacements match the average posterior scale. bb and ς\varsigma are both frozen before the posterior estimator is trained.

The hyperplane splits the batch into two groups that receive different displacements, so within a rule each measurement receives one reference point. Across the R rules of a step, each measurement receives R reference points. The switch rules satisfy both admissibility conditions in Definition 6: their reference points are dense in parameter space, and they can implement arbitrary half-space patches. The displacements have positive densities, so reference points come arbitrarily close to every point of Θ\Theta (R1). Every rule is a patch of two rules across a half-space, and every patch can be drawn, since the displacements, the direction and the position of the hyperplane are all drawn from distributions with full support (R2).

Prior and posterior rules.

Admissibility guarantees that the true posterior is the unique minimizer of the loss, but we observe that adding other rules helps training. A prior rule uses a single reference point drawn from the prior and shared by the batch. A posterior rule uses the MM posterior draws of each pair as reference points, detached from the computational graph. For the reference θ~m\tilde{\theta}_{m}, the credibility of θi\theta_{i} is computed from the M−1M-1 other draws. When a generated posterior sample is used as the reference point, that same sample must be excluded from the set of samples used to estimate the credibility value. Otherwise, the reference point would contribute a guaranteed zero-distance sample, changing the distribution of credibility values even when the estimator is correct.

Theorem 1 still applies.

Every term of the loss is nonnegative, and the switch rules keep a fixed share of the mixture, so the loss can only vanish if the loss restricted to switch rules vanishes, which forces qϕ=pq_{\phi}=p. The switch rules are essential for the theoretical guarantee, and the other two are supplementary choices intended to help optimization.

4.3 Relaxation of the indicator

To differentiate the loss with respect to ϕ\phi, we backpropagate through the sampler. For a diffusion model, we draw all the noises of the sampler in advance and hold them fixed, so that the sampler becomes a deterministic function of ϕ\phi. This is the reparameterization trick (Kingma and Welling, 2013). The exact credibility value is the fraction of generated samples whose distance from the reference point is no greater than the distance of the true signal. The indicator in this definition is nondifferentiable, so we replace it with a sigmoid approximation σ\sigma at temperature τ>0\tau>0, for θ~m∼qϕ(⋅∣y)\tilde{\theta}_{m}\sim q_{\phi}(\cdot\mid y),

sψ​(θ,y)≈1M​∑m=1Mσ⁡(d⁡(θ,ψ⁡(y))−d⁡(θ~m,ψ⁡(y))τ).s_{\psi}(\theta,y)\approx\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\sigma\!\left(\frac{d\big(\theta,\psi(y)\big)-d\big(\tilde{\theta}_{m},\psi(y)\big)}{\tau}\right). (10)

Algorithm 1 summarizes one training step, and Appendix B details its complexity.

5 Experiments

5.1 TARP-CvM as training signal

We first consider a setting in which the true posterior is known analytically. This experiment isolates the distinction between marginal coverage and posterior accuracy, allowing us to directly compare the minimizers of the HPD and TARP-CvM objectives. We illustrate Theorem 1 on a Gaussian linear inverse problem y=A​θ+εy=A\theta+\varepsilon, with a Gaussian prior and fewer measurements than parameters (Appendix E.1). The posterior is Gaussian, p⁡(θ∣y)=𝒩⁡(W∗​y,S∗)p(\theta\mid y)=\mathcal{N}(W^{*}y,S^{*}), and we fit a Gaussian estimator qϕ​(θ∣y)=𝒩⁡(W​y,S)q_{\phi}(\theta\mid y)=\mathcal{N}(Wy,S) by gradient descent on either an HPD-loss or TARP-CvM. The estimator is HPD-calibrated for every WW, provided that S=S∗+(W∗−W)​Σy​(W∗−W)⊤S=S^{*}+(W^{*}-W)\Sigma_{y}(W^{*}-W)^{\top}, where Σy\Sigma_{y} is the covariance of the measurements. Thus, an estimator with a biased conditional mean can still achieve correct HPD coverage if its covariance is sufficiently inflated. The HPD objective therefore admits a family of minimizers, including the prior, even though most of these distributions do not equal the true posterior. This manifold of minimizers contains the prior, at W=0W=0, and every point of it other than the posterior has a biased mean and a covariance wider than the posterior’s. Gradient descent on HPD coverage can therefore stop at any point of this manifold, not only at the posterior. With measurement-dependent references, TARP-CvM instead has the posterior as its unique minimizer (Theorem 1). In Figure 1, TARP-CvM recovers the posterior contours, whereas the HPD fit is biased and too conservative. The HPD coverage error cannot distinguish the two models, although their KL divergence to the posterior differs strongly.

5.2 Imaging inverse problems

We study posterior coverage calibration in high-dimensional posteriors on three inverse problems from InverseBench (Zheng et al., 2025). Each has the form y=𝒜⁡(θ)+εy=\mathcal{A}(\theta)+\varepsilon. These are linear inverse scattering (IS) and compressed-sensing MRI (MRI), whose forward operators are linear, and Navier–Stokes (NS), whose forward operator is nonlinear and only available as a black-box solver (Appendix E.3). For IS, ε\varepsilon is additive Gaussian noise. For MRI and NS, ε≡0\varepsilon\equiv 0, so the posterior has no density on the full signal space. On MRI, TARP-CvM therefore measures distances in the null space of AA, where Theorem 1 applies (Appendix E.3).

Unlike the plug-and-play methods InverseBench was designed for, we train fully amortized conditional models on pairs (θ,y)(\theta,y). The measurement is concatenated to the network input, as its adjoint reconstruction 𝒜⊤​y\mathcal{A}^{\top}y for IS and MRI, and at its native 64×6464\times 64 resolution for NS, which matches the resolution of the signal after 2×22\times 2 patching. All models are pretrained with denoising score matching (Song et al., 2021b, DSM,). They are then fine-tuned for 24k steps with one of four objectives, DSM alone (OPEN∅)\varnothing), a control that isolates the effect of additional training, or DSM plus a calibration regularizer, which is the energy score (ES), the pixel-wise CRPS (pCRPS), or TARP-CvM. All three regularizers use the same calibration batch, the same number of posterior samples per measurement, and the same T=20T=20-step DDIM sampler (Song et al., 2021a), through which gradients are backpropagated (see Appendix E.3 for details).

We measure coverage with the L1L^{1} TARP coverage error, ∫01|ECP⁡(qϕ,α,Rα,ψTARP)−α|​𝑑α\int_{0}^{1}|\mathrm{ECP}(q_{\phi},\alpha,R^{\text{TARP}}_{\alpha,\psi})-\alpha|\,d\alpha. We compute the coverage using standard binary indicators rather than the sigmoid relaxations used during training, and use the ℓ2\ell_{2} distance to define the TARP balls. We also use the Mira score (Sharief et al., 2026), which equals 2/32/3 for a calibrated model; values below the null band indicate overconfidence. For quality, we report in Table 3 the PSNR, SSIM, and relative L2L^{2} error of the posterior mean over K=32K=32 samples, the PSNR of a single draw, and the posterior spread (the per-pixel standard deviation across the KK samples, in physical units), all computed on 64 held-out observations, together with the DSM loss on the full validation split, averaged over three seeds.

All pretrained models are strongly overconfident (Mira between 0.51 and 0.61, Figure 3). Additional DSM training does not fix this, so the gains below come from the regularizers. On NS and IS, TARP-CvM gives the lowest coverage error (0.11 and 0.28, against 0.17 and 0.35 for the best scoring rule). On NS all three regularizers reach the Mira null band, but on IS only TARP-CvM does (0.68, against 0.53 for ES and 0.57 for pCRPS). On MRI, the two metrics disagree. ES has the lowest coverage error, but remains overconfident according to Mira, while TARP-CvM is the only method inside the band.

Increasing posterior variance can reduce the PSNR of individual posterior draws even when the posterior mean remains unchanged. This is not necessarily a deterioration in reconstruction accuracy: it can reflect the fact that the model is representing uncertainty that was previously missing. Calibration has little effect on the quality of generated samples. The validation DSM loss stays within 1%1\% of the control for every method. Posterior-mean PSNR is unchanged on IS and NS and drops by 0.80.8 dB on MRI. Per-draw PSNR drops more, by 0.350.35 to 1.91.9 dB, but this reflects the metric rather than accuracy. The expected squared error of a draw θ~∼q(⋅∣y)\tilde{\theta}\sim q(\cdot\mid y) decomposes as 𝔼⁡[‖θ~−θ∗‖2]=‖𝔼q​[θ~]−θ∗‖2+Varq​(θ~)\mathbb{E}\big[\|\tilde{\theta}-\theta^{*}\|^{2}\big]=\big\|\mathbb{E}_{q}[\tilde{\theta}]-\theta^{*}\big\|^{2}+\mathrm{Var}_{q}(\tilde{\theta}), where Varq​(θ~)=tr⁡Covq​(θ~)\mathrm{Var}_{q}(\tilde{\theta})=\operatorname{tr}\mathrm{Cov}_{q}(\tilde{\theta}) denotes the total variance, so a model that collapses its variance gains per-draw PSNR without improving its mean. Correct coverage requires nonzero variance, and TARP-CvM widens the posterior by 1515 to 58%58\% relative to the control, which lowers per-draw PSNR accordingly. On NS, the scoring rules instead improve the posterior mean by about 1 dB while slightly reducing the spread. This suggests that the pretrained model had errors due to both a biased mean, which the scoring rules correct, and insufficient spread, which TARP-CvM corrects. The wider spread of TARP-CvM may also partly compensate for residual error in the posterior mean.

Sampler depth.

Because the calibration term backpropagates through the sampler, training fixes the sampler depth, but any depth can be used at inference. We train with T=20T=20 and evaluate at T∈{20,100,500}T\in\{20,100,500\} (Figure 4). On NS and IS, Mira stays inside the null band at all depths, so calibration learned with a short chain survives at longer ones. On MRI, however, Mira decreases and leaves the null band at higher TT. At T = 100 and 500 it even falls below the DSM-only model, whose Mira improves with T. This suggests that on MRI part of the learned calibration compensates for the discretization error of the 20-step sampler rather than correcting the underlying score, so the correction no longer matches a finer discretization. In practice, the model should be sampled at the depth it was calibrated for, or calibrated at the depth used for inference, at a training cost that grows linearly with TT.

5.3 SBI benchmark

In contrast to the imaging experiments, the SBI benchmarks are low-dimensional problems for which standard NPE is already relatively well calibrated. Our objective is to establish that TARP-CvM can match a density-based calibration method while requiring only posterior samples. We evaluate our method on four problems from the SBI benchmark introduced in Hermans et al. (2022), namely SLCP, Weinberg, Spatial SIR and Lotka–Volterra, each at three simulation budgets {210,213,216}\{2^{10},2^{13},2^{16}\}. We compare conditional normalizing flows trained with Neural Posterior Estimation (Papamakarios and Murray, 2016; Lueckmann et al., 2017; Deistler et al., 2022; Greenberg et al., 2019, NPE,), with the HPD-based regularizer of CalNPE (Falkiewicz et al., 2023), and with TARP-CvM. In SBI, we usually only have access to samples from the simulator, and cannot evaluate the adjoint operator of the forward model. In order to get a point estimate b⁡(y)b(y) close to the posterior for reference points when only pairs of (θ,y)(\theta,y) are available, we train a multilayer perceptron (MLP) network targeting the posterior mean y↦𝔼p⁡(θ∣y)​[θ]y\mapsto\mathbb{E}_{p(\theta\mid y)}[\theta], with a mean-square-error loss, and freeze it during calibration of the posterior generative model. All methods share the same training protocol, with the same simulation budgets, validation set and checkpoint selection (Appendix E.2).

Under this matched protocol, NPE is already nearly calibrated on these low-dimensional problems. On the two TARP coverage maps, log posterior density and joint MMD on (θ,b⁡(y))(\theta,b(y)), a single method is significantly better than the other two in only two of the 48 comparisons: TARP-CvM on the switch map for Weinberg at 2102^{10}, and CalNPE on log density for Spatial SIR at 2102^{10} (Table 1, Appendix E.2).

TARP-CvM thus matches CalNPE using only posterior samples, without evaluating the density. Its log density does not differ significantly from that of NPE in any setting, but is lower than that of CalNPE on Spatial SIR at the two smaller budgets. CalNPE achieves a lower HPD coverage error, the statistic it optimizes, with a significant difference in four settings. On the independent Mira score, TARP-CvM is closest to the calibrated value 2/3 in half of the settings, and CalNPE deviates most from it in 10 of 12 settings, consistent with its conservativeness objective, a one-sided penalty on under-coverage that leaves over-coverage unpenalized, which we used to match the configuration reported by Falkiewicz et al. (2023). None of these differences is significant.

6 Conclusion

We introduced TARP-CvM, a differentiable coverage loss that vanishes if and only if the learned conditional distribution equals the true posterior. It requires only samples from the model, applies to any generative architecture, and is a strict divergence (Theorem 1). On SBI benchmarks, it matches a density-based coverage loss with the same number of model evaluations, without evaluating the density. On imaging inverse problems, including one with a nonlinear black-box forward model, it is the only regularizer that brings the posterior into the Mira null band on all three problems, with little change in the quality of point estimates. The main practical design choice is the construction of reference points, which are built around a point estimate b⁡(y)b(y). For linear forward models, the adjoint A⊤​yA^{\top}y works well. Without an adjoint, an auxiliary regressor of the posterior mean can be trained at extra cost, as in our SBI experiments. Future work includes other nonlinear inverse problems, such as full waveform inversion and black hole imaging, and SBI problems in cosmology, where the forward model is a physics simulator and posteriors are often multimodal.

Appendix A Proofs

This section proves Theorem 1. Section A.1 defines the support of a distribution over rules, Section A.2 recalls the notation, and Section A.3 collects preliminary facts: the regularity of the radial mass function, the calibration of the true posterior for every rule, and a Cramér–Wold argument showing that integrals over half-spaces determine a function of the measurement. The direction “qϕ=pq_{\phi}=p implies 𝒟ρ=0\mathcal{D}_{\rho}=0” holds for any ρ\rho and follows from Lemma 1. The converse is proved in three steps, one per subsection:

  1. (i)

    if 𝒟ρ=0\mathcal{D}_{\rho}=0, every rule in the support of ρ\rho is calibrated (Section A.4)

  2. (ii)

    by patching (R2), the coverage at each measurement then does not depend on the reference point (Section A.5)

  3. (iii)

    since reference points are dense (R1), this invariance forces p(⋅∣y)=qϕ(⋅∣y)p(\cdot\mid y)=q_{\phi}(\cdot\mid y) (Section A.6).

Section A.7 assembles the three steps.

A.1 Rules, their topology and the support of ρ\rho

A reference rule is a measurable map ψ:𝒴→Θ\psi:\mathcal{Y}\to\Theta. We define how far apart two rules ψ\psi and ψ′\psi^{\prime} are by

d0​(ψ,ψ′)=𝔼y∼p⁡(y)​[min⁡{1,‖ψ⁡(y)−ψ′​(y)‖}],d_{0}(\psi,\psi^{\prime})=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p(y)}\big[\min\{1,\|\psi(y)-\psi^{\prime}(y)\|\}\big],

the metric of convergence in probability. Two rules are close if their reference points are close for most measurements. The support of a distribution ρ\rho over rules is the set of rules that ρ\rho approaches arbitrarily closely with positive probability: ψ\psi is in the support if, for every ν>0\nu>0, a rule drawn from ρ\rho is within distance ν\nu of ψ\psi with positive probability,

suppρ={ψ:ℙψ′∼ρ[d0(ψ′,ψ)<ν]>0for every ν>0}.\operatorname{supp}\rho=\Big\{\psi:\ \mathbb{P}_{\psi^{\prime}\sim\rho}\big[d_{0}(\psi^{\prime},\psi)<\nu\big]>0\ \text{for every }\nu>0\Big\}.

A rule in supp⁡ρ\operatorname{supp}\rho need not be drawn with positive probability. For the switch sampler, any particular rule has probability zero, but rules arbitrarily close to it are drawn with positive probability.

Throughout the appendix we write qq for qϕq_{\phi}. The distance dd on Θ\Theta is induced by a norm, B⁡(c,t)={θ:d⁡(θ,c)≤t}B(c,t)=\{\theta:d(\theta,c)\leq t\} is the closed ball, and vol\mathrm{vol} is the Lebesgue measure on ℝdθ\mathbb{R}^{d_{\theta}}. By Assumption 1, Θ\Theta is open and, for every yy, p(⋅∣y)p(\cdot\mid y) and q(⋅∣y)q(\cdot\mid y) have continuous densities that are strictly positive on Θ\Theta. We recall the objects of the main text. For a reference point c∈Θc\in\Theta, the radial mass function of the estimator is

mc(t∣y)=ℙθ~∼q(⋅∣y)[θ~∈B(c,t)],t≥0.m_{c}(t\mid y)=\mathbb{P}_{\tilde{\theta}\sim q(\cdot\mid y)}\big[\tilde{\theta}\in B(c,t)\big],\qquad t\geq 0.

For a rule ψ\psi, the credibility value is sψ​(θ,y)=mψ⁡(y)​(d⁡(θ,ψ⁡(y))∣y)s_{\psi}(\theta,y)=m_{\psi(y)}\big(d(\theta,\psi(y))\mid y\big), the conditional coverage is Fψ(α∣y)=ℙθ∼p(⋅∣y)[sψ(θ,y)≤α]F_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y)=\mathbb{P}_{\theta\sim p(\cdot\mid y)}[s_{\psi}(\theta,y)\leq\alpha], and the expected coverage is Fψ​(α)=∫Fψ​(α∣y)​p​(y)​𝑑yF_{\psi}(\alpha)=\int F_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y)\,p(y)\,dy. Two remarks are used repeatedly. First, the conditional coverage at yy depends on the rule only through its reference point at yy: Fψ​(α∣y)=Fψ⁡(y)​(α∣y)F_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y)=F_{\psi(y)}(\alpha\mid y). Second, α↦Fψ​(α∣y)\alpha\mapsto F_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y) and α↦Fψ​(α)\alpha\mapsto F_{\psi}(\alpha) are cumulative distribution functions, hence non-decreasing and right-continuous.

We restate and prove Lemma 1.

Under Assumption 1, if q(⋅∣y)=p(⋅∣y)q(\cdot\mid y)=p(\cdot\mid y) for every yy, then Fψ​(α∣y)=αF_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y)=\alpha for every rule ψ\psi, every level α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] and every yy, and hence Fψ​(α)=αF_{\psi}(\alpha)=\alpha.

Lemma 2 (Radial mass function).

Under Assumption 1, for every yy:

  • (i)

    (c,t)↦mc​(t∣y)(c,t)\mapsto m_{c}(t\mid y) is continuous on Θ×[0,∞)\Theta\times[0,\infty);

Proof.

(i) Since Θ×[0,∞)\Theta\times[0,\infty) is a metric space, it suffices to check continuity along sequences. Let (cn,tn)n∈ℕ(c_{n},t_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} be a sequence converging to (c,t)(c,t). For every θ\theta with d⁡(θ,c)≠td(\theta,c)\neq t, the indicator 𝟏d⁡(θ,cn)≤tn\mathbf{1}_{d(\theta,c_{n})\leq t_{n}} converges to 𝟏d⁡(θ,c)≤t\mathbf{1}_{d(\theta,c)\leq t}. The sphere {θ:d⁡(θ,c)=t}\{\theta:d(\theta,c)=t\} has zero volume, hence zero mass under q(⋅∣y)q(\cdot\mid y), so the convergence holds qq-almost everywhere and dominated convergence gives mcn​(tn∣y)→mc​(t∣y)m_{c_{n}}(t_{n}\mid y)\to m_{c}(t\mid y). (ii) Since Θ\Theta is open, there is tc>0t_{c}>0 with B⁡(c,tc)⊆ΘB(c,t_{c})\subseteq\Theta. For 0≤t<t′≤tc0\leq t<t^{\prime}\leq t_{c}, the difference mc​(t′∣y)−mc​(t∣y)m_{c}(t^{\prime}\mid y)-m_{c}(t\mid y) is the qq-mass of the shell B⁡(c,t′)∖B⁡(c,t)B(c,t^{\prime})\setminus B(c,t), which has positive volume and lies in Θ\Theta, where q(⋅∣y)>0q(\cdot\mid y)>0. Hence it is positive. Finally mc​(0∣y)m_{c}(0\mid y) is the mass of the point cc, which is zero. ∎

Proposition 1 (Half-spaces detect functions).

Let ff be a bounded function on ℝdy\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}} such that

∫Hf⁡(y)​p​(y)​𝑑y=0for every half-space ​H={y:⟨u,y⟩≤t},\int_{H}f(y)\,p(y)\,dy=0\quad\text{for every half-space }H=\{y:\langle u,y\rangle\leq t\},

with uu a unit vector and t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}. Then f⁡(y)=0f(y)=0 for p⁡(y)p(y)-almost every yy.

Proof.

The idea is that integrals over half-spaces determine all integrals of functions of a projection ⟨u,y⟩\langle u,y\rangle, and these in turn determine the Fourier transform of f​pfp. Write g⁡(y)=f⁡(y)​p​(y)g(y)=f(y)\,p(y), which is integrable since ff is bounded, and fix a unit vector uu.

Slabs. Letting t→∞t\to\infty in the hypothesis gives ∫g=0\int g=0. Subtracting the hypothesis at two thresholds a<ba<b gives ∫{a<⟨u,y⟩≤b}g(y)dy=0\int_{\{a<\langle u,y\rangle\leq b\}}g(y)\,dy=0. Hence ∫h⁡(⟨u,y⟩)​g​(y)​𝑑y=0\int h(\langle u,y\rangle)\,g(y)\,dy=0 for every step function hh, that is, every finite combination of indicators of intervals (a,b](a,b].

Trigonometric functions. Fix λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}, κ>0\kappa>0 and n≥1n\geq 1. Let hnh_{n} be the step function equal to cos⁡(λ​a)\cos(\lambda a) on each interval (a,a+1/n](a,a+1/n] of a regular grid of [−κ,κ][-\kappa,\kappa], and to 00 outside [−κ,κ][-\kappa,\kappa]. Then |cos⁡(λ​s)−hn​(s)|≤|λ|/n|\cos(\lambda s)-h_{n}(s)|\leq|\lambda|/n for |s|≤κ|s|\leq\kappa, and ≤1\leq 1 otherwise, so

|∫cos(λ⟨u,y⟩)g(y)dy|=|∫(cos(λ⟨u,y⟩)−hn(⟨u,y⟩))g(y)dy|≤sup|f|(|λ|n+ℙy∼p[|⟨u,y⟩|>κ]).\Big|\int\cos(\lambda\langle u,y\rangle)\,g(y)\,dy\Big|=\Big|\int\big(\cos(\lambda\langle u,y\rangle)-h_{n}(\langle u,y\rangle)\big)\,g(y)\,dy\Big|\leq\sup|f|\Big(\frac{|\lambda|}{n}+\mathbb{P}_{y\sim p}\big[|\langle u,y\rangle|>\kappa\big]\Big).

Letting n→∞n\to\infty and then κ→∞\kappa\to\infty shows that the left-hand side is zero. The same argument applies to sin\sin, so ∫ei​λ​⟨u,y⟩​g​(y)​𝑑y=0\int e^{i\lambda\langle u,y\rangle}g(y)\,dy=0.

Conclusion. Every vector v∈ℝdyv\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}} is of the form λ​u\lambda u, so the Fourier transform g^​(v)=∫ei​⟨v,y⟩​g​(y)​𝑑y\hat{g}(v)=\int e^{i\langle v,y\rangle}g(y)\,dy vanishes everywhere. An integrable function whose Fourier transform vanishes is zero almost everywhere, so f⁡(y)​p​(y)=0f(y)\,p(y)=0 for almost every yy, that is, f⁡(y)=0f(y)=0 for p⁡(y)p(y)-almost every yy. This is the Cramér–Wold argument (Cramér and Wold, 1936). ∎

Half-spaces are used only through Proposition 1: any other family of sets for which this proposition holds can replace them in (R2).

A.5 From calibration to invariance to the reference point

Every rule in supp⁡ρ\operatorname{supp}\rho is now calibrated, but calibration is an average over measurements, in which errors at different measurements can cancel. This step obtains a statement at each measurement: the coverage curve at yy does not depend on the reference point. As in the main-text example, it compares a rule ψ′\psi^{\prime} with the rule patched from ψ\psi on a half-space, which isolates what happens on that half-space.

Lemma 5 (Invariance to the reference point).

Let ρ\rho be admissible with family Ψ\Psi, and suppose that every rule in supp⁡ρ\operatorname{supp}\rho is calibrated. Then, for p⁡(y)p(y)-almost every yy, the coverage curve at yy does not depend on the rule of Ψ\Psi:

Fψ​(α∣y)=Fψ′​(α∣y)for all ​ψ,ψ′∈Ψ​ and all ​α∈[0,1].F_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y)=F_{\psi^{\prime}}(\alpha\mid y)\qquad\text{for all }\psi,\psi^{\prime}\in\Psi\text{ and all }\alpha\in[0,1].
Proof.

Step 1: coverage of a patched rule. Fix ψ,ψ′∈Ψ\psi,\psi^{\prime}\in\Psi, a level α\alpha, and a half-space HH. The coverage at a measurement yy depends on the rule only through its reference point at yy. The patched rule ψ⊕Hψ′\psi\oplus_{H}\psi^{\prime} has reference point ψ⁡(y)\psi(y) for y∈Hy\in H and ψ′​(y)\psi^{\prime}(y) for y∉Hy\notin H, so its coverage curve at yy is Fψ​(α∣y)F_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y) on HH and Fψ′​(α∣y)F_{\psi^{\prime}}(\alpha\mid y) outside HH. Averaging over measurements,

Fψ⊕Hψ′(α)=∫HFψ(α∣y)p(y)dy+∫y∉HFψ′(α∣y)p(y)dy.F_{\psi\oplus_{H}\psi^{\prime}}(\alpha)=\int_{H}F_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y)\,p(y)\,dy+\int_{y\notin H}F_{\psi^{\prime}}(\alpha\mid y)\,p(y)\,dy.

Fψ⊕Hψ′(α)−Fψ′(α)=∫HΔ(y)p(y)dy,Δ(y)=Fψ(α∣y)−Fψ′(α∣y).F_{\psi\oplus_{H}\psi^{\prime}}(\alpha)-F_{\psi^{\prime}}(\alpha)=\int_{H}\Delta(y)\,p(y)\,dy,\qquad\Delta(y)=F_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y)-F_{\psi^{\prime}}(\alpha\mid y).

Here Δ⁡(y)\Delta(y) is the difference of coverage at yy between the two reference points ψ⁡(y)\psi(y) and ψ′​(y)\psi^{\prime}(y), and |Δ|≤1|\Delta|\leq 1.

Step 2: both rules are calibrated. The rule ψ′\psi^{\prime} is in supp⁡ρ\operatorname{supp}\rho because Ψ⊆supp⁡ρ\Psi\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\rho, and the patched rule ψ⊕Hψ′\psi\oplus_{H}\psi^{\prime} is in supp⁡ρ\operatorname{supp}\rho by (R2). Both are calibrated, so both coverages equal α\alpha and the left-hand side of Step 1 is zero:

∫HΔ⁡(y)​p​(y)​𝑑y=0for every half-space ​H.\int_{H}\Delta(y)\,p(y)\,dy=0\qquad\text{for every half-space }H.

Step 3: from half-spaces to each measurement. By Proposition 1, applied to f=Δf=\Delta, we get Δ⁡(y)=0\Delta(y)=0 for p⁡(y)p(y)-almost every yy. In other words, Fψ​(α∣y)=Fψ′​(α∣y)F_{\psi}(\alpha\mid y)=F_{\psi^{\prime}}(\alpha\mid y) for every measurement yy except those in a set Nψ,ψ′,αN_{\psi,\psi^{\prime},\alpha} that has probability zero under p⁡(y)p(y).

Step 4: all pairs and all levels at once. The exceptional set of Step 3 depends on ψ\psi, ψ′\psi^{\prime} and α\alpha. Let NN be the union of these sets over all pairs ψ,ψ′∈Ψ\psi,\psi^{\prime}\in\Psi and all rational levels α∈[0,1]∩ℚ\alpha\in[0,1]\cap\mathbb{Q}. There are countably many of them, so NN still has probability zero. For y∉Ny\notin N, the two coverage curves agree at every rational level. Both are distribution functions, hence right-continuous, and every α∈[0,1)\alpha\in[0,1) is a limit of rationals from the right, so they agree at every level; at α=1\alpha=1 both equal one. ∎

A.7 Proof of Theorem 1

Under Assumption 1 and for any admissible ρ\rho,

𝒟ρ(p,q)=0⇔q(⋅∣y)=p(⋅∣y)for p⁡(y)-almost every y.\mathcal{D}_{\rho}(p,q)=0\iff q(\cdot\mid y)=p(\cdot\mid y)\ \text{for $p(y)$-almost every }y.
Proof.

(⇐\Leftarrow) By Lemma 1, Fψ​(α)=αF_{\psi}(\alpha)=\alpha for every rule ψ\psi and every α\alpha, so Iψ=0I_{\psi}=0 for every ψ\psi and 𝒟ρ=0\mathcal{D}_{\rho}=0. This direction holds for any ρ\rho.

(⇒\Rightarrow) Suppose 𝒟ρ=0\mathcal{D}_{\rho}=0. By Lemma 4, every rule in supp⁡ρ\operatorname{supp}\rho is calibrated. By Lemma 5, there is a null set N2N_{2} outside which Fψ(⋅∣y)F_{\psi}(\cdot\mid y) is the same function for all ψ∈Ψ\psi\in\Psi. By (R1), there is a null set N1N_{1} outside which the reference points {ψ⁡(y):ψ∈Ψ}\{\psi(y):\psi\in\Psi\} are dense in Θ\Theta. For every y∉N1∪N2y\notin N_{1}\cup N_{2}, Lemma 6 applies and gives p(⋅∣y)=q(⋅∣y)p(\cdot\mid y)=q(\cdot\mid y). Since N1∪N2N_{1}\cup N_{2} is null, this holds for p⁡(y)p(y)-almost every yy. ∎

Appendix B Training algorithm

Algorithm 1 summarizes one training step with the TARP-CvM regularizer. The base loss ℒbase\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}} is the training objective of the generative model, such as denoising score matching for diffusion models or the negative log-likelihood for normalizing flows.

Complexity

For each rule, computing the NN credibility values requires N​MNM distance evaluations, and the closed-form statistic of Equation 5 only requires sorting them, at cost 𝒪⁡(N​log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(N\log N). Its gradient follows analytically from the ranks, so no differentiable sorting operator is needed. One step therefore costs 𝒪⁡(R​N​(M+log⁡N))\mathcal{O}\big(R\,N\,(M+\log N)\big) operations on top of drawing the N​MNM posterior samples. In practice, the cost is dominated by sampling. For a diffusion model with a TT-step sampler, a step requires N​M​TNMT network evaluations, and backpropagating through the chains that carry gradient multiplies their cost, and the memory they require, by a factor proportional to TT. Training cost thus grows linearly with the sampler depth, which is why we train with T=20T=20 (Section 5.2, Appendix E.3).

Iψ=∫01(Fψ​(α)−α)2​𝑑α.I_{\psi}=\int_{0}^{1}\big(F_{\psi}(\alpha)-\alpha\big)^{2}\,d\alpha.

Proposition 2 (Bias of the plug-in estimator).

Let s1,…,sNs_{1},\dots,s_{N}, with N≥2N\geq 2, be independent with common CDF FψF_{\psi} on [0,1][0,1]. Then
