Appendix D Scoring rules and loss landscapes

D.1 Definitions

The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) compares the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the model with the CDF of a point mass at the observation. Part of its appeal is that CDFs are easy to estimate from an ensemble of generated samples. For models that are easy to sample from but have no closed-form CDF, the CRPS admits the energy form

CRPS(qϕ(⋅|y),θ)=2𝔼θ^∼qϕ(⋅|y)|θ^−θ|−𝔼θ^,θ^′∼qϕ(⋅|y)|θ^−θ^′|.\mathrm{CRPS}(q_{\phi}(\cdot|y),\theta)=2\,\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\theta}\sim q_{\phi}(\cdot|y)}|\hat{\theta}-\theta|-\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\theta},\hat{\theta}^{\prime}\sim q_{\phi}(\cdot|y)}|\hat{\theta}-\hat{\theta}^{\prime}|.

The first term penalizes a model whose samples are far from the true θ\theta on average, and the second rewards samples that are spread out, so that a model cannot minimize the CRPS by collapsing to a point prediction.

Unlike CDFs, this energy form generalizes directly to several dimensions by replacing the absolute value with the Euclidean norm, which gives the energy score of Section 2. On the class of distributions with finite first moment, the energy score is strictly proper:

𝔼θ∼p(⋅∣y)[ES(qϕ(⋅|y),θ)]≥𝔼θ∼p(⋅∣y)[ES(p(⋅∣y),θ)],\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim p(\cdot\mid y)}[\mathrm{ES}(q_{\phi}(\cdot|y),\theta)]\geq\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim p(\cdot\mid y)}[\mathrm{ES}(p(\cdot\mid y),\theta)],

with equality if and only if qϕ(⋅|y)=p(⋅∣y)q_{\phi}(\cdot|y)=p(\cdot\mid y). Like CRPS, it can be evaluated from samples of a generative model alone.

In high dimension, the CRPS is often computed for each coordinate separately rather than replaced by the energy score. We call this the pixel-wise CRPS,

pCRPS(qϕ(⋅|y),θ)=∑j=1dθCRPS(qϕ(⋅|y)(j),θ(j)),\mathrm{pCRPS}(q_{\phi}(\cdot|y),\theta)=\sum_{j=1}^{d_{\theta}}\mathrm{CRPS}\big(q_{\phi}(\cdot|y)^{(j)},\theta^{(j)}\big),

where the superscript jj denotes restriction to the jj-th coordinate. Its motivation is often computational, since it parallelizes across pixels. It is however minimized by any model with the correct one-dimensional marginals, and therefore does not constrain the dependence between coordinates.

D.2 Strict propriety and training

Strict propriety is a statement about the global minimizer of the population loss, and two gaps separate it from what training achieves. First, the loss is minimized over a finite training set, and the minimizer of this empirical approximation need not be the minimizer of the population loss. Second, gradient descent generally finds local rather than global minima. Two strictly proper scoring rules share the same global minimizer, but they can have very different loss landscapes, with different local minima, so that training with one can yield much better coverage than training with the other. Section D.3 illustrates this on a Gaussian model.

D.3 Loss landscapes

We examine the same setting as the inverse problem in Fig. 1, setting θ\theta to have dimension 8 and YY dimension 4.

We identify the true parameters of the posterior distribution θ|Y\theta\mid Y and perturb them by deviating the mean in the direction of largest variance and the scale of the variance in that same direction. See the equation below for this perturbation model:

qa,b​(θ∣y)=Normal⁡(W∗​y+h⁡(a)​λj​vj,V​diag⁡(λ1,…,e2​b​λj,…,λD)​V⊤),q_{a,b}(\theta\mid y)=\operatorname{Normal}\left(W^{*}y+h(a)\sqrt{\lambda_{j}}v_{j},V\operatorname{diag}\left(\lambda_{1},\ldots,e^{2b}\lambda_{j},\ldots,\lambda_{D}\right)V^{\top}\right),

where a,ba,b are the mean and scale perturbation parameters, respectively. h⁡(a)=a3−3​a−4.048h(a)=a^{3}-3a-4.048 parameterizes the mean perturbation and vanishes at a=2.2a=2.2. The scale perturbation vanishes at b=0b=0. We see in Fig. 5 the loss landscapes for Energy Score and TARP-CvM in terms of aa and bb.

In Fig. 6, we have slices of the loss functions at the local and global minima of aa, the mean parameter. We see that TARP-CvM has much more sensitivity to changing the spread parameter, bb, when aa is at the local minimum than energy score does. In other words, we are comparing the steepness of the blue lines in each plot.

Intuitively, when one gets stuck in a local minimum for the mean parameter, TARP-CvM recovers correct coverage by pushing the conditional distribution toward wider spread to compensate for the bias in the mean. In contrast, the energy score’s loss function is relatively flat with respect to the spread parameter in this local optimum. So, when noisy gradients provide imperfect optimization of this population loss, the energy score is less likely to correct coverage when gradient descent is near a local minimum for the conditional mean, since the signal in the loss is too flat to overcome gradient noise.

Appendix E Experiments

E.1 Toy model

Setup

The parameters have a Gaussian prior θ∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ0)\theta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{0}), and the measurements follow y=A​θ+εy=A\theta+\varepsilon, with ε∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​I)\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I), dy=4d_{y}=4, and dθ=8d_{\theta}=8, so that AA cannot be inverted. The posterior is Gaussian,

p⁡(θ∣y)=𝒩⁡(W∗​y,S∗),W∗=Σ0​A⊤​Σy−1,S∗=Σ0−W∗​A​Σ0,p(\theta\mid y)=\mathcal{N}(W^{*}y,\,S^{*}),\qquad W^{*}=\Sigma_{0}A^{\top}\Sigma_{y}^{-1},\qquad S^{*}=\Sigma_{0}-W^{*}A\Sigma_{0},

where Σy=A​Σ0​A⊤+σ2​I\Sigma_{y}=A\Sigma_{0}A^{\top}+\sigma^{2}I is the covariance of the measurements. The estimator is qϕ​(θ∣y)=𝒩⁡(W​y,S)q_{\phi}(\theta\mid y)=\mathcal{N}(Wy,S), where ϕ=(W,S)\phi=(W,S) are parameters to fit.

HPD calibration does not identify the posterior

The density of qϕ(⋅∣y)q_{\phi}(\cdot\mid y) is a decreasing function of the Mahalanobis norm m⁡(θ)=(θ−W​y)⊤​S−1​(θ−W​y)m(\theta)=(\theta-Wy)^{\top}S^{-1}(\theta-Wy), so its HPD regions are the ellipsoids {θ:m⁡(θ)≤tα}\{\theta:m(\theta)\leq t_{\alpha}\} with mass α\alpha under qϕ(⋅∣y)q_{\phi}(\cdot\mid y). Under p⁡(θ,y)p(\theta,y), the residual e=θ−W​ye=\theta-Wy decomposes as (θ−W∗​y)+(W∗−W)​y(\theta-W^{*}y)+(W^{*}-W)y. The first term has distribution 𝒩⁡(0,S∗)\mathcal{N}(0,S^{*}) given yy, hence is independent of yy, and the second has covariance (W∗−W)​Σy​(W∗−W)⊤(W^{*}-W)\Sigma_{y}(W^{*}-W)^{\top}, so that marginally

e∼𝒩⁡(0,CW),CW=S∗+(W∗−W)​Σy​(W∗−W)⊤.e\sim\mathcal{N}(0,C_{W}),\qquad C_{W}=S^{*}+(W^{*}-W)\,\Sigma_{y}\,(W^{*}-W)^{\top}.

If S=CWS=C_{W}, the residual of the true parameter has the same distribution as θ~−W​y\tilde{\theta}-Wy for a draw θ~∼qϕ(⋅∣y)\tilde{\theta}\sim q_{\phi}(\cdot\mid y). The true parameter then falls in each HPD region with probability α\alpha, so the estimator is HPD-calibrated, for every WW.

Points of the manifold

At W=W∗W=W^{*}, S=S∗S=S^{*} is the true posterior. At W=0W=0, S=S∗+W∗​Σy​W∗⁣⊤=S∗+W∗​A​Σ0=Σ0S=S^{*}+W^{*}\Sigma_{y}W^{*\top}=S^{*}+W^{*}A\Sigma_{0}=\Sigma_{0}, so the prior is HPD-calibrated. For every W≠W∗W\neq W^{*}, the mean W​yWy is biased and S−S∗=(W∗−W)​Σy​(W∗−W)⊤S-S^{*}=(W^{*}-W)\Sigma_{y}(W^{*}-W)^{\top} is positive semi-definite and nonzero, so the estimator is wider than the posterior at every measurement: marginal calibration is reached by trading the bias of the mean for extra spread.

E.2 Simulation Based Inference

Problems.

We use the simulators of Hermans et al. (2022) with the problem settings of Falkiewicz et al. (2023). For each problem we generate up to 2162^{16} simulations for training, with 10410^{4} for validation, and 10410^{4} held-out pairs for evaluation.

  • •

    SLCP (simple likelihood, complex posterior) is used in the marginal variant of Hermans et al. (2022), in which only two parameters are inferred and the likelihood becomes intractable. The parameters are θ∈[−3,3]2\theta\in[-3,3]^{2}. The observation y∈ℝ8y\in\mathbb{R}^{8} consists of four draws from a bivariate Gaussian with fixed mean (0.7,−2.9)(0.7,-2.9), standard deviations θ12\theta_{1}^{2} and θ22\theta_{2}^{2}, and correlation tanh⁡(ρ)\tanh(\rho), where nuisance parameter ρ∼𝒰⁡(−3,3)\rho\sim\mathcal{U}(-3,3) is marginalized out. Since θ\theta enters only through its squares, the posterior has four symmetric modes.

  • •

    Weinberg infers the Fermi constant, normalized to its nominal value, θ∈[0.25,2]\theta\in[0.25,2], from y∈[−1,1]20y\in[-1,1]^{20}. The observation contains the cosines of the scattering angle of twenty e+​e−→μ+​μ−e^{+}e^{-}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-} events drawn by rejection sampling from the differential cross-section at a beam energy of 4040 GeV.

  • •

    Spatial SIR infers the infection and recovery rates θ=(β,γ)∈[0,1]2\theta=(\beta,\gamma)\in[0,1]^{2} of a stochastic epidemic on a 50×5050\times 50 lattice. The epidemic is seeded with 1+Poisson⁡(3)1+\mathrm{Poisson}(3) infected cells at random positions and propagated through 3 ×\times 3 neighborhoods. The observation y∈{0,1}3×50×50y\in\{0,1\}^{3\times 50\times 50} records the susceptible, infected and recovered state of every cell at time t=1t=1.

  • •

    Lotka–Volterra is a predator-prey Markov jump process started from 5050 predators and 100100 prey. The parameters θ∈[−4,1]2\theta\in[-4,1]^{2} are the log-rates of the two predator reactions. The two prey log-rates are drawn from the same prior and marginalized out. The observation y∈ℝ2×1001y\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 1001} is the trajectory of both populations.

Architecture and training.

Neural posterior estimation (Papamakarios and Murray, 2016; Lueckmann et al., 2017; Deistler et al., 2022; Greenberg et al., 2019, NPE,) fits a conditional density estimator qϕ​(θ∣y)q_{\phi}(\theta\mid y) by maximum likelihood on simulated pairs, minimizing −(1/N)∑ilogqϕ(θi∣yi)-(1/N)\sum_{i}\log q_{\phi}(\theta_{i}\mid y_{i}). This is equivalent to minimizing the forward KL divergence to the posterior, averaged over p⁡(y)p(y). We use the architecture of Falkiewicz et al. (2023), implemented with the sbi library (Tejero-Cantero et al., 2020). It is a conditional neural spline flow (Durkan et al., 2019), with rational-quadratic spline transforms (10 bins, hidden width 64) and a Gaussian base distribution. There are three transforms, each a coupling layer followed by a linear layer, except for the one-dimensional Weinberg problem, which uses a single transform whose spline parameters depend on the conditioning only. The flow is conditioned on an embedding of yy given by an MLP with three hidden layers of width 64, SELU activations and a 10-dimensional output. The 7500-dimensional Spatial SIR observations and the 2002-dimensional Lotka-Volterra trajectories are flattened before embedding.

Parameters and observations are standardized per coordinate using the training data. We train with Adam, using a learning rate of 10−310^{-3}, a batch size of 128, gradient-norm clipping at 5, for 50 epochs without early stopping. We keep the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss on the 10410^{4} validation simulations. All three objectives of Table 1 share this training recipe.

For CalNPE, we use the conservativeness objective of Falkiewicz et al. (2023), which penalizes only coverage below the nominal level, with weight λ=100\lambda=100, the default of their released code, instead of the published λ=5\lambda=5, which gave worse results in our experiments. HPD credibilities are estimated from the density of the estimator at 16 draws from the prior, with straight-through gradients for the indicators and differentiable sorting (Blondel et al., 2020).

TARP-CvM uses weight λ=30\lambda=30 and M=16M=16 reparameterized posterior draws per pair, so that both regularizers use 1616 flow evaluations per pair: CalNPE evaluates the density at 1616 prior draws, TARP-CvM draws 1616 posterior samples. Each step uses R=48R=48 references in three groups of 1616, described below. The indicators are relaxed with a sigmoid at temperature τ=0.05\tau=0.05 times the median sample-to-reference distance of each reference, treated as a constant, and the loss is the closed-form CvM statistic of Equation 5, computed per reference and averaged over the RR references.

Reference points without a forward operator

Without access to the forward operator to estimate b⁡(y)b(y), we resort to regressing the posterior mean. The point estimate b⁡(y)b(y) is an MLP (two hidden layers of width 128, SELU) trained beforehand on the flow’s own training pairs with a mean-squared-error loss, with AdamW (learning rate 10−310^{-3}, weight decay 10−410^{-4}, batch 256). The R=48R=48 references of a step form three groups of 1616: (1) switch-rule references, (2) points drawn from the prior distribution and shared by the batch, and (3) the posterior draws of each pair, detached from the computation graph. The credibility of a posterior reference is computed from the 1515 other draws, so that sis_{i} remains uniform when qϕ=pq_{\phi}=p, by exchangeability.

E.3 Imaging inverse problems

Problems

We selected three inverse problems introduced in InverseBench (Zheng et al., 2025). They all have the form y=𝒜⁡(θ)+εy=\mathcal{A}(\theta)+\varepsilon, where yy are measurements, AA is a forward model, θ\theta is the signal we seek to reconstruct and ε\varepsilon additive noise.

  • •

    Navier–Stokes (NS). θ\theta is the initial vorticity of a 2D incompressible flow on (0,2​π)2(0,2\pi)^{2} with periodic boundary conditions (128×128128\times 128 pixels, Reynolds number 200, forcing f⁡(x)=−4​cos⁡(4​x2)f(x)=-4\cos(4x_{2})), obtained by evolving a draw from 𝒩⁡(0,(−Δ+9​I)−4)\mathcal{N}\big(0,(-\Delta+9I)^{-4}\big) for five time units. The forward operator is 𝒜=P∘L\mathcal{A}=P\circ L, where the solution operator LL, computed with a black-box pseudo-spectral solver, maps θ\theta to the vorticity at time T=1T=1 and is nonlinear. The subsampling operator PP keeps one grid point out of two in each direction, giving 64×6464\times 64 noise-free observations.

  • •

    Linear inverse scattering (IS). θ\theta is a 128×128128\times 128 permittivity contrast map of HL60 cell nuclei, generated with the simulator of Wiesner et al. (2019). Under the first Born approximation, 𝒜=A\mathcal{A}=A is linear, with 2020 transmitters and 360360 receivers on a circle of radius 1.61.6 m, and noise level σy=10−4\sigma_{y}=10^{-4}, resampled at every training batch.

  • •

    Compressed sensing MRI (MRI). θ\theta is a complex 320×320320\times 320 knee image from fastMRI (Zbontar et al., 2018), a coil-combined minimum-variance unbiased estimate (Jalal et al., 2021), stored as two real channels. Since these images have no coil sensitivity maps, we use the single-coil operator 𝒜=P​F\mathcal{A}=PF, with FF the orthonormal 2D Fourier transform and PP a ×4\times 4 subsampling mask that keeps 8080 of the 320320 vertical k-space lines (2525 central lines and 5555 random outer lines, redrawn for every example). The measurements are noise-free.

We did not select the Black hole imaging problem because no training set of images is publicly available, and we did not select Full waveform inversion, because it did not fit the shared setup of conditioning architecture with fixed image-shape. Our method is nonetheless applicable to these problems as well.

Noise-free measurements

On MRI and NS, measurements are noise-free, so the posterior is supported on the set {θ:𝒜⁡(θ)=y}\{\theta:\mathcal{A}(\theta)=y\} and has no density on ℝdθ\mathbb{R}^{d_{\theta}}, which Assumption 1 requires. For the linear MRI operator, writing θ=A+​y+z\theta=A^{+}y+z with z=(I−A+​A)​θz=(I-A^{+}A)\theta, the range component A+​yA^{+}y is fixed by the measurement, and the posterior is a distribution over the null-space component zz, which has a density on the null space of AA. Restricted to this subspace, the null-space distance d⁡(θ,θ′)=‖(I−A+​A)​(θ−θ′)‖d(\theta,\theta^{\prime})=\|(I-A^{+}A)(\theta-\theta^{\prime})\| is a norm, so Theorem 1 applies to the posterior of zz given yy, with Θ\Theta replaced by the null space. This is why TARP-CvM uses this distance on MRI. On NS, the solution set of the nonlinear operator has no such linear parametrization, and Theorem 1 does not strictly apply. There, the experiment tests the loss beyond its assumptions, and the Mira score, which requires no density, still measures coverage. On IS, the measurement noise gives the posterior a density, as Assumption 1 requires.

Diffusion models

Diffusion models (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020) map the target distribution p⁡(x)p(x) to white Gaussian noise by progressively perturbing the data xx through a diffusion process. Following Song et al. (2021b), we express the continuous diffusion process as a stochastic differential equation (SDE):

d​xt=f⁡(xt,t)​d​t+g⁡(t)​d​wt,dx_{t}=f(x_{t},t)dt+g(t)dw_{t},

where xt∈ℝNx_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} is the perturbed data at time tt, f⁡(xt,t)∈ℝNf(x_{t},t)\in\mathbb{R}^{N} is the drift coefficient, g⁡(t)∈ℝ+g(t)\in\mathbb{R}_{+} is the diffusion coefficient, and wt∈ℝNw_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} is a standard Wiener process. This SDE admits a reverse process, mapping noise to the target distribution:

d​xt=[f⁡(xt,t)−1+η22​g​(t)2​∇xt​log⁡pt​(xt)]​d​t+η​g​(t)​d​w¯t,dx_{t}=\big[f(x_{t},t)-\frac{1+\eta^{2}}{2}g(t)^{2}\nabla_{x_{t}}\log p_{t}(x_{t})\big]dt+\eta g(t)d\bar{w}_{t},

where w¯\bar{w} is a standard Wiener process when time flows backward. Among the different kinds of diffusion processes, we used the Variance Exploding schedule, which parametrizes the noising kernel xt∼𝒩⁡(αt​x,σt2​𝕀N)x_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\alpha_{t}x,\sigma_{t}^{2}\mathbb{I}_{N}), with αt=1\alpha_{t}=1, log⁡σt=(1−t)​log⁡σmin+t​log⁡σmax\log\sigma_{t}=(1-t)\log\sigma_{\min}+t\log\sigma_{\max}, with σmin=10−3\sigma_{\min}=10^{-3} and σmax=102\sigma_{\max}=10^{2}. We also adopt the preconditioning strategy of Karras et al. (2022), which parametrizes a denoising network dϕd_{\phi} instead of the score function.

Our target distribution is the conditional distribution of x=θ|yx=\theta\mid y, where yy are measurements and θ\theta is the signal we aim to recover. The measurement yy enters as a fixed image, concatenated channel-wise to the noisy input of the network. For both MRI and IS, we compute the adjoint solution to transform measurement into images A⊤​yA^{\top}y. NS observations are already 64×6464\times 64 images, the resolution of the signal after 2×22\times 2 patching, so they are concatenated to the patched input without resampling. NS has no linear adjoint, so the switch rules use the nearest-neighbor upsampled observation as the point estimate b⁡(y)b(y). We describe all our choices for the network architectures and training strategies in Table 2. All fine-tuning runs share the calibration batch (16 pairs per step on NS, 8 otherwise), the sampler depth (T=20T=20), the optimizer, the number of steps, and the sampler chains that carry gradients (Mgrad=2M_{\mathrm{grad}}=2 per pair on NS and MRI, 88 on inverse scattering). λ\lambda is tuned once on Navier–Stokes and reused for IS and MRI (λ=10\lambda=10 for TARP-CvM and λ=0.003\lambda=0.003 for ES and pCRPS).

On one NVIDIA GH200, a fine-tuning step takes 1.91.9 s with TARP-CvM against 0.70.7 s with the energy score or pCRPS on NS, 1.01.0 s against 0.70.7 s on IS, and 3.73.7 s against 2.62.6 s on MRI, a 1.41.4 to 2.7×2.7\times increase in training time with respect to the ES and pCRPS, and an 1818 to 33×33\times increase with respect to DSM alone. Figure 7 shows example observations and target ground truth signals for the three inverse problems.
